lessons.title: Orderings, fences and happens-before
lessons.summary: Choose counter ordering and trace synchronisation edges across threads.
lessons.body:
Memory order is part of the algorithm’s correctness argument. The store-buffering test starts two atomic variables at zero; each thread stores one to its own variable and then loads the other.

## The C11 orderings

| Order | Guarantee | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `relaxed` | atomic only | counters |
| `acquire` | later ops stay later | lock, read flag |
| `release` | earlier ops stay earlier | unlock, publish |
| `acq_rel` | both, for RMW | CAS in a lock |
| `seq_cst` | one global order | default |

C11 also defines `memory_order_consume`. Mainstream compiler implementations have generally strengthened it to acquire; avoid relying on a cheaper dependency-only mapping without checking the compiler and language version.

**Sequentially consistent** (`seq_cst`) is the default for every atomic operation without `_explicit`. All `seq_cst` operations appear in a single total order agreed by every thread. Using seq_cst for all four operations in this litmus test forbids both loads seeing zero. Other correctly constructed synchronization protocols or fence placements can also forbid it. For ordinary scalar atomics, x86 compilers commonly implement a sequentially consistent store using `xchg` or a suitable fenced sequence. Costs depend on hardware, contention and surrounding code; no universal timing ratio is asserted.

Relaxed is fine when you need the value to be correct but nothing else to be ordered with it, such as a statistics counter read after all threads are joined.

> [!tip] Default to seq_cst
> Use the default orderings until a profiler proves the fence matters. Weaker orderings are an optimisation with a high cost in reasoning, and bugs in them often appear only on one architecture under load.

## Fences

A **fence** (memory barrier) orders memory operations without being attached to a particular variable: `atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_seq_cst)` in C11. Hardware equivalents include x86 `mfence` and ARM `dmb ish`. The Linux kernel has its own family (`smp_mb()`, `smp_wmb()`, `smp_rmb()`, `smp_store_release()`, `smp_load_acquire()`), documented at length in `memory-barriers.txt`.

There is also a **compiler-only barrier**, such as `asm volatile("" ::: "memory")` in GCC, which stops the compiler moving accesses across it but emits no instruction.

## Happens-before

The formal model ties this together. The **happens-before** relation is built from:

1. **Sequenced-before**: within one thread, program order.
2. **Synchronises-with**: a release store and an acquire load that reads its value; an unlock and a later lock of the same mutex; `pthread_create` and the start of the new thread; a thread's end and `pthread_join` returning.
3. **Transitivity**: happens-before chains, as the formula below shows.

Writing an arrow for "happens-before":

```formula
A → B and B → C gives A → C
where
A: an operation in some thread, such as a write, a read, a lock or an unlock
B: a second operation
C: a third operation, possibly in yet another thread
→: happens-before: the operation on the left is guaranteed to be ordered before, and visible to, the operation on the right
In words: ordering links join up, so if A is ordered before B and B before C, then A is ordered before C, even when A and C share no direct synchronisation.
```

The earlier message-passing unit supplies one such chain. The write `data = 42` is sequenced-before the release store; the release store synchronises-with the acquire load that reads 1; the acquire load is sequenced-before the read of `data`. Chaining the three edges gives "the write of 42 happens-before the read", so if the consumer reaches the print, it prints 42.

The rule that matters: if a write happens-before a read of the same location (and no other write intervenes), the read sees that write. If two conflicting accesses are **not** ordered by happens-before and are not both atomic, you have a data race, and in C, C++ and Rust that is undefined behaviour. Java and Go define similar happens-before rules; Java gives racy programs weaker but defined semantics rather than UB.

## Key takeaways

- Relaxed counters need no payload-publication edge when the final read follows thread joins.
- Using sequentially consistent operations throughout the store-buffering test excludes the both-zero result.
- Happens-before chains through sequenced-before and synchronises-with; elapsed time alone supplies no edge.

## Further reading

- [C11 draft: memory model and atomics](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [Linux memory barriers](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/wrappers/memory-barriers.html)
- [The Double-Checked Locking declaration](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~pugh/java/memoryModel/DoubleCheckedLocking.html)
- [Java memory model specification](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)
- [Python free-threading guidance](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html)
- [The Go memory model](https://go.dev/ref/mem)

questions.prompt: Worker threads increment `atomic_long bytes_sent` after every write. The main thread reads it only after joining all workers, to print a total. Which memory order is sufficient for the increments?

options.text: `memory_order_seq_cst`, because anything weaker can lose increments
options.explanation: All memory orders, including relaxed, keep the read-modify-write atomic. Ordering is about *other* memory operations, not about losing updates.

options.text: `memory_order_acquire`, so the main thread sees the latest value
options.explanation: Acquire is a valid RMW order, but it is stronger than necessary here. The joins supply the required final-observation ordering; no producer publication is needed from the increments.

options.text: `memory_order_relaxed`
options.explanation: Correct. Each increment must be atomic, but nothing else is published with it. `pthread_join` already makes every worker's operations happen-before the main thread's read.

options.text: None; a plain `long` is fine because the main thread reads after join
options.explanation: The workers race with *each other* during the run, so a plain `long` loses updates and is undefined behaviour.

questions.workedExample:
1. Requirement 1: no lost increments. Any atomic RMW gives that, even relaxed.
2. Requirement 2: does any other data depend on seeing this counter? No; it is a statistic.
3. Requirement 3: does the main thread see the final value? Thread termination synchronises-with `pthread_join` returning, so yes.
4. So `atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&bytes_sent, n, memory_order_relaxed)` is enough.

Supported scalar x86 RMW mappings often use the same locked instruction for these orders. AArch64 code generation varies with target features, primitive and compiler; inspect it before drawing a performance conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which of these create a **happens-before** edge from an operation in thread A to an operation in thread B? Select all that apply.

options.text: A unlocks mutex `m`; later B locks `m`
options.explanation: Correct. An unlock synchronises-with the next lock of the same mutex, so everything A did before unlocking is visible to B after locking.

options.text: A does a release store to `flag`; B does an acquire load of `flag` that reads A's value
options.explanation: Correct. This is the defining synchronises-with pair.

options.text: A does a relaxed store to `flag`; B does a relaxed load that reads it
options.explanation: Relaxed operations are atomic but create no ordering. B sees `flag` but has no guarantee about A's other writes.

options.text: A calls `pthread_create` to start thread B
options.explanation: Correct. Everything A did before `pthread_create` happens-before the start of B.

options.text: A writes `x` and B reads `x` a second later in wall-clock time
options.explanation: Wall-clock time is not a happens-before relation. Without synchronisation, this is a data race regardless of how much time passes.

questions.workedExample:
Happens-before = sequenced-before within a thread, plus synchronises-with between threads, closed under transitivity.

Synchronises-with sources:

1. Mutex unlock → subsequent lock of the same mutex (A).
2. Release store → acquire load that reads it (B).
3. Thread creation → thread start (D); thread end → join return.

Relaxed atomics (C) give atomicity only. Time (E) gives nothing: the formal model has no clock, which is why "it ran much later, so it must see the write" is not a valid argument.

questions.prompt:
To fix the store-buffering test, a developer makes `x` and `y` atomic and uses **release stores** and **acquire loads**:

```
T1: store(x, 1, release)
    r1 = load(y, acquire)
T2: store(y, 1, release)
    r2 = load(x, acquire)
```

Is `r1 == 0 && r2 == 0` now impossible?

options.text: Yes: acquire and release forbid all reordering
options.explanation: A release stops *earlier* operations moving after the store; an acquire stops *later* operations moving before the load. Neither stops a later acquire load moving ahead of an earlier release store.

options.text: Yes, but only on x86
options.explanation: On x86 these compile to plain `mov`s, and plain `mov`s are exactly what produced (0, 0) in the first place.

options.text: No, and it can never be prevented on x86
options.explanation: It can: seq_cst stores compile to `xchg` (or `mov` + `mfence`), which drains the store buffer first.

options.text: No: both-zero remains allowed; use all seq_cst operations or a correctly placed seq_cst fence between store and load in each thread
options.explanation: Correct. If both acquire loads read the initial zero, neither reads the other release, so no such synchronizes-with edge connects them. All-seq_cst operations forbid that cycle; properly placed fences can also do so.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each release store precedes an acquire load in its own thread.
2. If both loads read their initial zero, neither observes the other thread’s release, so those operations establish no cross-thread synchronises-with edge.
3. The language model therefore permits both-zero; acquire/release alone does not forbid the store-buffering outcome.
4. Making all four operations sequentially consistent forbids that cycle. Properly placed sequentially consistent fences can also do so.
5. For supported ordinary scalar x86 atomics, compilers commonly use xchg or a suitable fenced store sequence; inspect the actual target rather than assuming one universal instruction.

lessons.title: Make lazy initialisation safe
lessons.summary: Repair double-checked locking and use documented initialisation mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Treat any pointer/field sequence as an illustrative failure of an invalid C program: the unlocked plain pointer access races with publication. With classic double-checked locking on a plain pointer, thread A is inside the lock running `instance = make();`. Thread B calls `get()`. What is the dangerous outcome?

options.text: B creates a second instance
options.explanation: B either sees NULL and blocks on the lock (then sees A's pointer on its second check), or sees non-NULL. It does not get past the inner check with NULL while A holds the lock.

options.text: B deadlocks on the lock
options.explanation: A releases the lock after initialising, so B would just wait briefly. Deadlock is not the issue.

options.text: B always waits for the lock, making the fast path useless
options.explanation: Once `instance` is set, B skips the lock. The problem is that it can skip it too early.

options.text: B sees a non-NULL `instance` before the object's fields are visible, skips the lock, and uses a partly initialised object
options.explanation: Correct as an illustrative incomplete-publication symptom. The plain pointer data race makes the C program undefined, so 0 or garbage in a field is not an exhaustive outcome set. Use valid atomic publication and lifetime rules, or a standard once-initialisation API.

questions.workedExample:
`instance = make()` is really:

```
p = malloc(...)
p->a = 1; p->b = 2   (init)
instance = p         (publish)
```

1. Without a release, the publish may become visible first.
2. B's outer check reads `instance` without the lock and without acquire. It sees non-NULL.
3. B returns `p` and reads `p->a`: may be 0 or garbage.

Fix: release store when publishing, acquire load in the outer check (or `pthread_once`, a C++ magic static, a Java `volatile`).

lessons.title: Progress guarantees and CAS retries
lessons.summary: Separate blocking, obstruction-free, lock-free and wait-free progress and trace a maximum update.
lessons.body:
Locks are simple and correct, but they have one structural weakness: **if the thread holding a lock stops, everyone waiting for it stops too**. The holder might be preempted, page-faulting, running a signal handler, or simply slow. Under heavy load that one stalled thread sets the pace for all the others.

Lock-free techniques avoid holding anything that others must wait for. Instead of "acquire, modify, release", threads prepare a change privately and publish it with a single atomic instruction, retrying if someone else got there first. This lesson covers how that works, why it is much harder than it looks, and the more practical read-mostly tools (read-write locks, seqlocks and RCU) that real kernels and servers rely on.

## Progress guarantees

"Lock-free" has a precise meaning. It describes what happens when threads are delayed, not whether the code contains the word `lock`.

| Guarantee | Promise |
|---|---|
| Blocking | a stalled thread can stop all |
| Obstruction-free | a thread alone finishes |
| Lock-free | some thread always progresses |
| Wait-free | every thread finishes, bounded |

- **Blocking algorithm**: any algorithm using a mutex. If the holder is descheduled, nobody else in that critical section progresses.
- **Obstruction-free**: a thread finishes in a bounded number of steps if all others pause. Contending threads may keep undoing each other's work.
- **Lock-free**: continued execution guarantees system-wide operation progress under the algorithm's primitive and scheduling assumptions. An individual operation can starve; this is not a fixed wall-clock completion deadline.
- **Wait-free**: *every* thread completes in a bounded number of its own steps, however others behave. The strongest guarantee and the hardest to build.

A spinlock built from CAS is **not** lock-free: if the holder is preempted, every spinner makes zero progress. Using atomic instructions does not by itself make an algorithm lock-free.

Maurice Herlihy showed in 1991 that primitives differ in power. Plain loads and stores, or test-and-set, cannot build wait-free versions of every data structure for arbitrary numbers of threads; compare-and-swap (and LL/SC) can. That is why CAS is the foundation of everything in this lesson.

## The CAS retry loop

The example keeps a maximum with an initial floor of zero: values below zero do not lower that floor. The basic lock-free pattern is: read the current value, compute a new one privately, and CAS it in. On comparison failure, another update changed the expected value; a weak CAS may also fail spuriously. Reload/recompute as the algorithm requires.

```c
#include <stdatomic.h>

atomic_long max_seen = 0;

void record(long v) {
    // Retry only while our value is larger.
    long cur = atomic_load(&max_seen);
    while (v > cur &&
           !atomic_compare_exchange_weak(
               &max_seen, &cur, v))
        ;  // cur now holds the new value
}
```

On failure, C11's CAS writes the value it found into `cur`, so the loop re-tests with fresh data. Assuming lock-free atomic primitives and their required forward progress, the loop has system-wide non-blocking progress. A comparison mismatch shows interference; a weak CAS can also fail spuriously, so not every failed call proves another operation succeeded.

CAS retry loops generally do not give each thread a fixed retry bound. By contrast, a fetch-add implemented as one native instruction has a bounded number of algorithmic steps, assuming that primitive completes. This is not a bound on wall-clock latency: scheduling, faults and hardware contention still matter.

## Key takeaways

- A spinlock remains blocking even when it uses compare-and-swap.
- Lock-free gives system-wide progress, while wait-free bounds each operation’s own steps under its assumptions.
- Non-spurious comparison failure indicates interference; weak CAS may also fail spuriously.

## Further reading

- [Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization](https://cs.brown.edu/~mph/Herlihy91/p124-herlihy.pdf)
- [Michael–Scott queue paper](https://www.cs.rochester.edu/u/scott/papers/1996_PODC_queues.pdf)
- [Linux RCU documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/RCU/whatisRCU.html)
- [Linux sequence counters and seqlocks](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/locking/seqlock.html)
- [Userspace RCU](https://liburcu.org/)
- [Python threading](https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)

questions.prompt: A stack data structure is protected by a spinlock built from compare-and-swap. The thread holding the spinlock is preempted for 50 ms in the middle of a push. Which progress guarantee does this design provide?

options.text: Wait-free
options.explanation: Wait-free means every thread finishes in a bounded number of its own steps. Here every waiter spins for the full 50 ms making no progress at all, so it is nowhere near wait-free.

options.text: Lock-free, because it is built from CAS rather than a mutex
options.explanation: This confuses the instruction with the guarantee. Lock-free means *some* thread always progresses; while the holder is suspended, no thread can complete an operation, whatever instruction the lock uses.

options.text: Blocking: a stalled holder stops every other thread
options.explanation: Correct. Any algorithm in which one suspended thread can prevent all others from completing is blocking. A spinlock is a lock, even when it is written with CAS.

options.text: Obstruction-free
options.explanation: Obstruction-free requires that a thread running alone can finish. A waiter running alone still cannot finish, because the suspended holder owns the lock.

questions.workedExample:
Ask the defining question for each guarantee: *if some threads stop, can the others still finish?*

1. Holder suspended mid-push.
2. Every other thread spins on the lock word. None can enter, so none completes a push or pop.
3. That rules out obstruction-free (a lone thread cannot finish), lock-free (no thread progresses) and wait-free.
4. So it is a **blocking algorithm**.

The lesson: "lock-free" is about what happens when threads are delayed, not about which instructions appear in the code. A Treiber stack is lock-free because nobody ever holds anything others must wait for.

questions.prompt:
`max_seen` starts at 5 and uses the lesson's CAS loop:

```c
long cur = atomic_load(&max_seen);
while (v > cur &&
       !atomic_compare_exchange_weak(
           &max_seen, &cur, v))
    ;
```

T1 calls `record(9)` and T2 calls `record(7)`. Both load `cur = 5`. T2's CAS runs first and succeeds; then T1's CAS runs. What is the final value of `max_seen`? Assume both calls complete, no other writes occur, and the stated first CAS succeeds.

options.explanation: This assumes T1's failed CAS ends its call. In fact the failure refreshes `cur` to 7, T1 re-tests `9 > 7` and tries again.
Correct if both calls complete. T1’s comparison failure refreshes cur to 7; it retries while 9 is larger, and eventual successful completion leaves 9. Weak CAS may require extra attempts.
Both CAS operations compare against a real value of `max_seen`, and T2's succeeded, so the value cannot still be 5.

options.text: Either 7 or 9, depending on timing
options.explanation: With the stated completed calls and no other writes, the final maximum is 9 in every interleaving. A losing operation retries only while its proposed maximum is larger; this is not a bounded elapsed-time guarantee.

questions.workedExample:
Trace it:

```
max_seen = 5
T1: cur = 5      T2: cur = 5
T2: CAS(5 -> 7)  ok,  max_seen = 7
T1: CAS(5 -> 9)  fails, cur = 7
T1: 9 > 7, CAS(7 -> 9) ok
max_seen = 9
```

The key C11 detail is that a failed `compare_exchange` writes the value it actually found into `cur`, so the loop condition re-tests with fresh data. If T2 had been recording 12 instead, T1 would see `9 > 12` is false and stop without writing, which is also correct.

questions.prompt: For algorithmic claims, assume suitable lock-free primitive progress and sound node-publication, lifetime and reuse protocols; separate allocator costs are outside this model. Which statements about progress guarantees are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A Treiber stack is lock-free: if one thread is suspended between reading `top` and its CAS, others can still push and pop
options.explanation: Correct. The suspended thread holds nothing. Others' CAS operations succeed; when it resumes, its CAS fails (or, with ABA protection, behaves correctly) and it retries.

options.text: A stack data structure protected by a glibc futex-based mutex is lock-free, because the fast path never enters the kernel
options.explanation: The fast path is about speed, not progress. If the mutex holder is suspended, every other thread waits, which is blocking.

options.text: In a CAS update loop, a non-spurious comparison failure can show that another thread changed the expected value
options.explanation: Correct (ignoring the spurious failures `_weak` permits). The value only changes because another thread wrote it, which is exactly why the loop is lock-free.

options.text: Assuming native fetch-add completes, a counter increment implemented by one x86 fetch-add has a bounded number of algorithmic steps
options.explanation: Correct under the stated primitive-progress assumption: there is no software retry loop. This does not guarantee bounded elapsed time under arbitrary scheduling or hardware contention.

options.text: A CAS-loop counter is wait-free, because CAS is a single atomic instruction
options.explanation: Each CAS is bounded, but the loop is not: an unlucky thread can keep losing the race forever. That makes it lock-free, not wait-free.

questions.workedExample:
Use the definitions:

- **Lock-free**: continuing system execution guarantees operation completion under the algorithm’s primitive and scheduling assumptions.
- **Wait-free**: every thread finishes in bounded steps.

1. Treiber stack: a stalled thread blocks no one. Lock-free. True.
2. Futex mutex: a stalled holder blocks everyone. Blocking. False.
3. A non-spurious CAS comparison failure shows interference; weak CAS may also fail spuriously.
4. Under the stated native-instruction completion assumption, the fetch-add increment has bounded algorithmic steps. True.
5. CAS loop: one thread can fail indefinitely. Only lock-free. False.

lessons.title: Treiber stack and the ABA trap
lessons.summary: Trace pointer publication and an old next pointer that survives a changed-then-restored top.

questions.prompt: Trace pointer identities in this deliberately unsafe algorithm sketch, rather than treating it as a defined C output guarantee. A Treiber stack in C holds `A → B → C`. T1 begins `pop`, reads `old = A` and `next = B`, and is preempted before its CAS. T2 pops A, pops B, frees B, and then pushes A back. T1 resumes and runs `CAS(&top, A, B)`. What is `top` afterwards?

options.text: B, a node T2 has already freed; C is no longer reachable from `top`
options.explanation: Correct. `top` equals A again, so the CAS succeeds and installs T1's stale `next`. The Treiber stack now starts at memory that was already freed and C has been lost. This is the ABA problem.

options.text: A, because T1's CAS fails when it notices the Treiber stack has changed
options.explanation: CAS only compares the current value with the expected one. `top` changed from A to B to C and back to A; it cannot tell, so it succeeds.

options.text: C, because T1's CAS fails, refreshes `old` and retries
options.explanation: That would happen if the CAS failed, but `top` holds the same pointer value T1 expects. Nothing in the comparison reveals that the Treiber stack underneath has changed.

options.text: NULL, because T2 emptied the Treiber stack
options.explanation: T2 pushed A back, so the Treiber stack was `A → C` when T1 resumed, not empty.

questions.workedExample:
Follow `top` and the list step by step:

```
start        top=A  A->B->C
T1 reads     old=A, next=B
T2 pop       top=B  B->C
T2 pop       top=C  C
T2 free(B)
T2 push(A)   top=A  A->C
T1 CAS(A,B)  A==A, so top=B
```

1. When T1 resumes, `top` is A, exactly what it expects.
2. The CAS swaps in `next`, which was computed from the *old* state: B.
3. B has been freed, and C (still on the real Treiber stack) is now unreachable.

The value went A, then other values, then A again. Comparing values cannot detect that.

lessons.title: Retire nodes before freeing them
lessons.summary: Separate address-reuse ABA from the earlier dereference that may already access freed memory.
lessons.body:
In a Treiber pop, a thread first loads the atomic top pointer, then reads the node’s next field, then attempts CAS. Another thread must not free or recycle that node between the first two steps.

## Safe memory reclamation

The second bug on the `(!)` line is a **use-after-free**. Between T1 loading `old` and reading `old->next`, T2 may have popped that node and freed it. T1 then reads memory that was already freed, which may crash or return garbage, even if the CAS later fails.

With a sound shared-lock and lifetime protocol, removal/freeing and every relevant dereference are coordinated. A lock protects nothing if some accesses or frees ignore it. Without one, you need a way to know when **no thread can still be looking at a node**. The main schemes are:

| Scheme | Idea |
|---|---|
| Garbage collection | freed only when unreachable |
| Hazard pointers | threads announce what they read |
| Epoch-based | free after all threads move on |
| RCU | free after an RCU grace period |

- **Garbage collection** prevents freeing a node or recycling its address while a live reference remains. It does not prevent logical ABA if the program explicitly removes and reinserts the same node, so node-reuse rules still matter. This removes one reclamation burden in managed runtimes, while logical reuse still needs an algorithmic argument. `java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue` is based on the **Michael–Scott queue** (1996), which uses CAS on both the head and the tail.
- **Hazard pointers** (Maged Michael, 2004): before dereferencing a node, a thread publishes its address in a per-thread "hazard" slot and re-checks it is still reachable. A thread that wants to free a node first scans everyone's hazard slots and defers the free if it finds a match.
- **Epoch-based reclamation** (used by Rust's `crossbeam-epoch`): threads mark themselves as active in a global epoch; retired nodes are freed once every active thread has moved past the epoch in which they were retired. This can reduce per-access announcement work compared with hazard pointers, but the cost depends on the implementation and workload; one stalled pinned thread can prevent epoch advancement and delay reclamation.

WG21 adopted P2530R3 (hazard pointers) and P2545R4 (RCU) into the C++ working paper at the June 2023 Varna meeting. The proposed hazard_pointer and rcu headers still require an appropriate language/library implementation; check its actual interface and availability before relying on them.

## Key takeaways

- Reading a removed node before CAS can already be a use-after-free.
- Hazard pointers and epoch schemes delay reuse while a reference could remain live.
- A reclamation scheme also needs valid publication and node-reinsertion rules; finite tags alone are insufficient.

## Further reading

- [Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization](https://cs.brown.edu/~mph/Herlihy91/p124-herlihy.pdf)
- [Michael–Scott queue paper](https://www.cs.rochester.edu/u/scott/papers/1996_PODC_queues.pdf)
- [Linux RCU documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/RCU/whatisRCU.html)
- [Linux sequence counters and seqlocks](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/locking/seqlock.html)
- [Userspace RCU](https://liburcu.org/)
- [Python threading](https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)
- [WG21 editor report: June 2023 adopted motions](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2023/n4959.html)

questions.prompt: Assume every node removed from a C Treiber stack is retired and never explicitly reinserted while stale readers can retain it. Which techniques can address address-reuse ABA when implemented correctly? Assume a version tag cannot wrap while an observation is outstanding.

options.text: Declare `top` as `volatile`
options.explanation: `volatile` only forces real memory accesses. It neither makes the CAS see history nor stops a node's memory being reused, so ABA is untouched.

options.text: Pair `top` with a version counter and update both with a 16-byte CAS (`cmpxchg16b`)
options.explanation: Correct. Every successful update bumps the counter, so "A at version 7" no longer matches "A at version 9" and T1's stale CAS fails.

options.text: Use `atomic_compare_exchange_strong` instead of `_weak`
options.explanation: The strong form only removes spurious failures. It still compares the pointer value and still succeeds when A has come back.

options.text: Hazard pointers with publish-then-revalidate before dereference, and retirement that forbids reclamation/reuse while protected
options.explanation: Correct. A node that T1 is examining cannot be freed and reused, so it cannot reappear at `top` as a different incarnation while T1 holds it.

options.text: Epoch-based reclamation, so a popped node's memory is not reused while any thread that might have read it is still active
options.explanation: Correct. Like hazard pointers, it stops addresses being recycled while a stale reference may exist, which removes the reuse that makes ABA possible.

questions.workedExample:
ABA needs two ingredients: (1) CAS compares only the current value, and (2) the same value (address) reappears while someone holds a stale copy.

| Option | Breaks which ingredient? |
|---|---|
| volatile | neither |
| tagged pointer | 1: value now includes a version |
| strong CAS | neither |
| hazard pointers | 2: no reuse while held |
| epochs | 2: no reuse while held |

In practice reclamation schemes are preferred, because they also fix the use-after-free on `old->next`, which tags alone do not.

questions.prompt: A developer adds a 64-bit version tag to `top` and uses a 16-byte CAS, so the Treiber stack is now safe from ABA. Popped nodes are released with `free()`. Under load the program still occasionally crashes inside `pop`. Why?

options.text: `cmpxchg16b` is not truly atomic on multicore x86
options.explanation: For a supported, correctly aligned operand and target, locked cmpxchg16b provides an atomic 16-byte comparison and exchange. That protects the comparison, not the earlier dereference or the node’s lifetime.

options.text: The 64-bit tag wraps around and lets ABA through
options.explanation:
A 64-bit tag takes a very long time to wrap:

```formula
t_wrap = 2^64 / r
t_wrap = 2^64 / (10^9 /s)
t_wrap ≈ 1.84 × 10^10 s
t_wrap ≈ 584.5 years
where
t_wrap: the time until the tag returns to a value it held before
2^64: 2 to the power 64, the number of distinct 64-bit tag values, about 1.84 × 10^19
r: the update rate: 10^9 updates per second
10^9: 10 to the power 9, one billion
s: second
years: years of 365.25 days (31,557,600 s)
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: at a billion updates a second, a 64-bit tag takes over five centuries to repeat.
```

This illustrates a very long cycle, but finite tags are not a mathematical no-wrap guarantee. The immediate dereference-after-free bug needs no wraparound.

options.text: The CAS ignores the tag on some cores
options.explanation: A 16-byte CAS compares all 16 bytes; there is no core that compares only the pointer half.

options.text: Between loading `old` and reading `old->next`, another thread can pop and `free()` that node; the tag makes the later CAS fail, but the read of the freed node has already happened
options.explanation: Correct. The unsafe dereference precedes the tag comparison. A finite tag also needs a wraparound argument; even a non-wrapping tag cannot keep a removed node alive. A valid hazard, epoch or other reclamation protocol must delay freeing it.

questions.workedExample:
Look at the order of operations in `pop`:

```
1  old  = top        (ptr, tag)
2  next = old->next  <- reads node
3  CAS(top, old, next)
```

1. T1 does step 1 and is preempted.
2. T2 pops the same node and calls `free()`. The allocator may unmap the page or hand the memory to another caller.
3. T1 does step 2: it dereferences memory that was already freed. Crash, or garbage in `next`.
4. Step 3 would fail thanks to the tag, but the damage happened at step 2.

So the Treiber stack needs **safe memory reclamation**: do not free a node until no thread can still be between steps 1 and 3 with a pointer to it.

lessons.title: When read-write locks help
lessons.summary: Compare concurrent read work with shared reader-metadata overhead.

questions.prompt: A service on a 32-core machine replaces a mutex around a hash-map lookup with a `pthread_rwlock_t`. Lookups take about 100 ns and make up 99.9% of operations. Throughput barely improves. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: `pthread_rwlock_rdlock` makes a system call every time, so readers are slow
options.explanation: Like mutexes, glibc's rwlocks take a user-space fast path with atomic instructions when they can. The cost here is not syscalls.

options.text: Writers are starving the readers
options.explanation: A low write count does not alone rule out long writer hold times. The question illustrates reader-metadata contention as a plausible cause; measurement must distinguish it from writer delays.

options.text: glibc read-write locks only let one reader in at a time
options.explanation: Readers do share the lock. The problem is what each reader has to do to get in.

options.text: A plausible cause is coherence traffic from shared reader-metadata updates dominating the short useful lookup
options.explanation: Correct as a hypothesis to test. Many read-write-lock implementations update shared reader metadata, so short reads can spend much of their time on coherence traffic. The hypothetical lookup duration and write percentage do not prove that this is the measured bottleneck.

questions.workedExample: A plausible bottleneck is atomic modification of shared rwlock metadata on reader entry/exit. That coherence traffic can dominate very short useful work. The hypothetical 100 ns lookup is not a measured cache-transfer latency, and write frequency alone does not prove writer hold times are harmless. Profile the implementation before choosing RCU, sharding or another protocol.

lessons.title: Validate seqlock snapshots
lessons.summary: Use an even unchanged sequence value to decide whether a retry-safe copy is usable.
lessons.body:
A short update to several plain values can overlap a reader’s copy. A sequence counter lets a reader detect that overlap and discard the speculative copy under a memory model that permits the protocol.

## Seqlocks

A **seqlock** lets readers proceed without writing anything. The writer increments a sequence counter before and after each update, so the counter is odd while a write is in progress. Readers read the counter, read the data, then read the counter again, and retry if it was odd or has changed.

```text
writer (writers serialised by a lock):
  increment sequence counter: now odd
  update the protected fields
  increment sequence counter: even again

reader:
  read the initial sequence counter
  retry if it is odd
  copy the protected fields
  read the final sequence counter
  accept only if even and unchanged
```

The acceptance rule can be expressed precisely. This model assumes the counter cannot wrap back to the same value during one read attempt:

```formula
(s_start mod 2) = 0
s_end = s_start
where
s_start: the sequence-counter value read before copying the fields
s_end: the sequence-counter value read after copying the fields
mod: modulo, the remainder after integer division; a remainder of zero on division by two means the count is even
In words: accept the copy only when both conditions hold: the first count is even, and the final count matches it. For example, counts ten and twelve require a retry despite both being even.
```


This is algorithm pseudocode. Portable C requires a race-free representation (for example atomic fields) plus a proven ordering protocol; retrying does not undo undefined behavior. Linux seqlock APIs follow the Linux kernel memory model and do not magically make arbitrary plain C fields portable atomic objects. Writers must also meet the API's serialization and non-preemption requirements.

These readers do not take the writer lock or update a shared reader count, reducing contention. They do not scale perfectly: cache traffic and repeated retries still cost time. The cost: a reader may read torn, inconsistent data and must throw it away and retry, so it must never follow pointers inside that data (they might point to memory that was already freed). Seqlocks suit small, plain values updated often and read constantly. Linux timekeeping uses sequence-counter protocols for consistent snapshots. Clock-specific fast paths, tickless operation and clocksource handling differ; not every clock query or time update follows one universal path.

## Key takeaways

- Accept a copy only when the sequence value was even and is unchanged.
- Readers may need retries and must not dereference pointers that an update could invalidate.
- Portable C and kernel seqlock implementations need their own proven race-free/order protocols.

## Further reading

- [Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization](https://cs.brown.edu/~mph/Herlihy91/p124-herlihy.pdf)
- [Michael–Scott queue paper](https://www.cs.rochester.edu/u/scott/papers/1996_PODC_queues.pdf)
- [Linux RCU documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/RCU/whatisRCU.html)
- [Linux sequence counters and seqlocks](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/locking/seqlock.html)
- [Userspace RCU](https://liburcu.org/)
- [Python threading](https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)

questions.prompt: A seqlock reader reads the sequence counter and gets 10, copies the protected data, then reads the counter again and gets 12. What should it do?

options.text: Accept the copy, because both counter values are even
options.explanation: Even values only show that no write was in progress at the two instants checked. A whole write (10 → 11 → 12) happened in between, so the copy may be torn.

options.text: Discard the copy and retry, because a write happened while it was copying and the data may mix old and new fields
options.explanation: Correct. The counter changed, so the reader cannot trust what it copied. It loops and tries again; readers never block the writer, they just redo their work.

options.text: Block until the writer releases its lock, then use the copy
options.explanation: Seqlock readers do not wait on the writer's lock, and waiting would not make the stale copy valid. They simply retry the read.

options.text: Use the copy, since 12 is newer than 10
options.explanation: The value of the counter does not validate data copied before it changed. The copy could contain half of the old record and half of the new one.

questions.workedExample:
The reader's rule is: *the copy is valid only if the counter was even and unchanged across the whole copy.*

```
read seq   -> 10  (even: no write now)
copy data  ...    writer: 10->11,
                  updates, 11->12
read seq   -> 12  (changed!)
```

1. 10 is even, so it was safe to start.
2. 12 is not equal to 10, so a write completed during the copy.
3. The copy might be torn (for example new seconds with old nanoseconds), so discard it and loop.

This is why seqlock readers must never follow pointers in the data: a torn copy could contain a pointer to memory that was already freed.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical 32-bit kernel reads a split 64-bit timestamp frequently and updates it in a short timer-interrupt section. Assume a proven kernel memory-model implementation, serialized non-preempted writers and retry-safe reads. Which listed technique is a good fit without allocating a new object per update?

options.text: A read-write lock, so readers can share it
options.explanation: A read-write lock can provide safety, but shared reader-metadata traffic can reduce its benefit for a very brief snapshot. The prompt does not establish an exact read rate or measured bottleneck.

options.text: A seqlock: the writer bumps a sequence counter around each update, and readers retry if it was odd or changed
options.explanation: Correct under the prompt’s proven kernel protocol and retry-safe data assumptions. Readers validate an even unchanged sequence counter without taking the writer’s exclusion lock; retry and coherence costs still exist.

options.text: RCU: allocate a new timestamp object for each update and publish it with an atomic pointer swap
options.explanation: An allocated immutable snapshot with valid RCU publication and reclamation could be safe, but violates the requested approach of avoiding a new allocation per update. No particular update frequency is established by the prompt.

options.text: No synchronisation: writes are rare, so readers almost always see a correct value
options.explanation: On a 32-bit CPU the value is read in two halves. A reader that runs between the writer's two stores combines halves from different times, which can be wildly wrong when the low half carries into the high half.

questions.workedExample:
Match the data to the tool:

1. **Small, plain data** (8 bytes, no pointers): a torn copy is harmless if it is detected and thrown away.
2. **Read constantly, written often but briefly**: readers must never write shared state.
3. That is exactly a seqlock's niche.

Why torn reads matter here:

```
old = 0x00000001_FFFFFFFF
new = 0x00000002_00000000
reader: high = 1 (old)
writer: stores both halves
reader: low  = 0 (new)
result  0x00000001_00000000
```

How far off is that?

```formula
v_new − v_torn = 2^33 − 2^32
v_new − v_torn = 2^32 ≈ 4.3 × 10^9 ticks
where
v_new: the new timestamp 0x00000002_00000000, which equals 2^33 ticks (high half 2, low half 0)
v_torn: the value the reader assembled, 0x00000001_00000000, which equals 2^32 ticks
2^32: 2 to the power 32, the weight of 1 in the high half: 4,294,967,296
2^33: 2 to the power 33, twice 2^32
ticks: timer ticks, the counting unit of the timestamp
≈: approximately equal to
10^9: 10 to the power 9, one billion
In words: the torn read lands about 4.3 billion ticks below the true value.
```

The seqlock reader sees the counter changed and retries.

lessons.title: RCU publication and grace periods
lessons.summary: Publish a replacement object and wait for pre-existing readers before reclamation.

questions.prompt: An RCU writer has built a new version of a configuration object and published it with `rcu_assign_pointer`. Why must it call `synchronize_rcu()` (or `call_rcu()`) before freeing the old version?

options.text: Because `rcu_assign_pointer` is asynchronous and the pointer has not actually changed yet
options.explanation: The publication API supplies the ordering needed for readers that observe the replacement. The grace period protects readers of the removed version; it is not a timer for making one pointer assignment finish.

options.text: Because freeing memory is only allowed while holding the RCU read lock
options.explanation: There is no such rule; in fact freeing inside a read-side critical section would defeat the purpose. The writer frees the old copy after readers are done with it.

options.text: Because every reader starting after synchronize_rcu is invoked must also finish before it can return
options.explanation: The RCU guarantee need not wait for read-side sections that begin after synchronize_rcu is invoked. It must account for all pre-existing sections that might retain the removed object.

options.text: Because readers that started before the publish may still hold a pointer to the old version and be reading it
options.explanation: Correct. A reader can retain the old reference across the update. Safe reclamation waits until every relevant pre-existing read-side section has ended; the writer’s publication alone does not establish that lifetime fact.

questions.workedExample:
1. Reader R can load the old pointer before the writer removes that object from the shared structure.
2. Publication of a replacement does not finish R’s existing read-side critical section.
3. Freeing immediately can therefore invalidate R’s retained reference.
4. synchronize_rcu waits for all read-side critical sections pre-existing its invocation; call_rcu schedules reclamation after the corresponding grace period. Subsequent sections need not delay that grace period.

The core guarantee concerns sections present at the grace-period wait, rather than a blanket assertion that every reader starting later in wall-clock time must immediately observe the newest pointer. Correct RCU publication, reader and lifetime APIs remain necessary.

questions.prompt:
Timeline of an RCU-protected structure:

```
t=0  R1: rcu_read_lock()
t=1  R2: rcu_read_lock()
t=2  R1: rcu_read_unlock()
t=3  W: rcu_assign_pointer(new)
     W: synchronize_rcu()
t=4  R3: rcu_read_lock()
t=5  R2: rcu_read_unlock()
t=6  R3: rcu_read_unlock()
```

Which readers must `synchronize_rcu()` wait for before it may return?

options.text: Only R2
options.explanation: Correct. R2 is the only listed read-side section active at the synchronize_rcu invocation. R1 already exited and R3 begins later, so R3 need not delay this grace period. R2’s exit at time five is a lower bound, not a promised completion time.

options.text: R1, R2 and R3
options.explanation: R1 has already left its read-side section when the wait is invoked. R3 begins afterward and need not be included. R2 is the only listed section active at invocation that the grace-period guarantee must cover.

options.text: R2 and R3, because both are active when `synchronize_rcu()` is called
options.explanation: R3 is not active at invocation and need not delay this grace period. R2 was active then; whether later sections overlap in wall-clock time does not change that pre-existing-section requirement.

options.text: None, because readers hold no locks the writer can see
options.explanation: RCU supplies a mechanism to account for pre-existing readers. The details depend on the flavour and kernel configuration; they can include quiescent states and explicit tracking of preempted readers.

questions.workedExample: At the synchronize_rcu invocation (t=3), R1 has already exited and R2 is active. R2 must finish before the wait may complete. R3 starts afterward and is not necessarily included. Thus t=5 is a lower bound, not a promised return time; batching and scheduling can delay completion.

lessons.title: Publish immutable snapshots in Python
lessons.summary: Use a brief lock for publication and keep previously returned versions unchanged.
lessons.body:
The useful RCU idea here is an unchanged published version. A managed runtime helps preserve object lifetime, while a documented lock supplies the publication protocol in this Python example.

### The same idea in Python

Managed runtimes help keep referenced objects alive, but do not supply publication ordering or application immutability automatically. This example uses a brief shared lock to obtain or publish a snapshot, then allows use of that immutable snapshot outside the lock.

```python
import threading

_config = {"timeout": 10}  # never mutated
_write_lock = threading.Lock()

def get_config():
    with _write_lock:
        return _config  # immutable snapshot

def set_timeout(t):
    global _config
    with _write_lock:      # publish lock
        # Shallow copy: nested values must
        # also
        # remain immutable to readers.
        new = dict(_config)
        new["timeout"] = t
        _config = new      # publish
```

Readers briefly take the publication lock, then retain a reference to an unchanged dictionary. Reclamation timing is runtime-dependent. Callers must never mutate the returned dictionary or mutable objects reachable from it. Java’s `CopyOnWriteArrayList` similarly provides snapshot iteration using replacement arrays for mutative operations; frequent copying can make it unsuitable for write-heavy workloads.

The rule that makes this safe: **never mutate a published object**. `_config["timeout"] = 30` could break the guarantee that a published dictionary never changes; do not equate Python multi-step-operation races with the precise C data-race definition.

> [!note] Content gap
> No hardware-specific lock, cache-transfer or RCU timing benchmark is available. The Treiber stack example deliberately omits safe reclamation, and the seqlock/RCU fragments are protocol illustrations, not complete production implementations.

## Choosing a tool

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Shared counter | atomic fetch-add |
| Small, hot, plain data | seqlock |
| Read-mostly linked data | RCU or copy-on-write updates |
| Long reads, some writes | read-write lock |
| Queue between threads | library queue |
| Anything else | a mutex |

> [!warning] Lock-free is not automatically faster
> Under heavy contention on one word, CAS loops fail and retry repeatedly, and the cache line still bounces between cores. A well-implemented mutex that puts waiters to sleep can beat a naive lock-free structure. Lock-free code is also very hard to get right and test. Use proven libraries (`java.util.concurrent`, Rust's `crossbeam`, Folly, Boost.Lockfree, `liburcu`) and benchmark before replacing a lock.

## Key takeaways

- Build a private replacement and publish it under the shared lock.
- A retained reference keeps an old dictionary alive, but the application must also keep it unchanged.
- This lock-assisted snapshot example is not a lock-free Python RCU implementation.

## Further reading

- [Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization](https://cs.brown.edu/~mph/Herlihy91/p124-herlihy.pdf)
- [Michael–Scott queue paper](https://www.cs.rochester.edu/u/scott/papers/1996_PODC_queues.pdf)
- [Linux RCU documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/RCU/whatisRCU.html)
- [Linux sequence counters and seqlocks](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/locking/seqlock.html)
- [Userspace RCU](https://liburcu.org/)
- [Python threading](https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)

questions.prompt:
The lesson's Python copy-on-write config is changed so the writer updates two fields **in place**:

```python
def move(host, port):
    with _write_lock:
        # Changes an already shared
        # dict.
        _config["host"] = host
        # May run after a reader uses
        # host.
        _config["port"] = port
```

Readers still do `c = get_config()` and then `connect(c["host"], c["port"])`. What can fail?

options.text: Nothing: each dict assignment is atomic under the GIL, so the update is safe
options.explanation: Even if an individual operation has runtime-level protection, a pair of updates is not a portable atomic snapshot. The invariant requires immutable publication or synchronized reads of the entire pair.

options.text: Readers deadlock because they do not take `_write_lock`
options.explanation: get_config now takes a brief publication lock. That does not deadlock this protocol; the defect is that returned dictionaries may be mutated later while readers use them outside the lock.

options.text: A reader can run between the two assignments and connect to the new host with the old port
options.explanation: Correct. Readers share the same dict the writer is mutating, so a reader can observe the half-updated state. Building a new dict and replacing the reference publishes both fields at once.

options.text: Python raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`
options.explanation: That error only occurs when iterating a dict while its size changes. The reader indexes two keys, and the writer changes values, not the size.

questions.workedExample: A reader first gets a reference to the current dictionary and releases the brief publication lock. The writer then changes host in that same dictionary, the reader reads host and port before the second assignment, and the writer finally changes port. The reader can therefore combine versions. Instead, build a replacement dictionary under the publication lock and leave every previously returned dictionary unchanged. The same rule extends to nested mutable values.
